items.followUp: State two more principles of cell theory.

rubric.why: This is one of the central principles of cell theory.
rubric.description: States that all organisms are made of one or more cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that organisms consist of cells.

rubric.why: This identifies the cell as the fundamental unit of life.
rubric.description: States that the cell is the basic structural and/or functional unit of life.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the cell as the basic unit of structure or function.

modelAnswer: All organisms are composed of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

items.followUp: What did Rudolf Virchow add to the cell theory?

rubric.why: Schleiden's conclusion concerned the cellular composition of plants.
rubric.description: States that Schleiden concluded plants are made of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking Schleiden with plants being composed of cells.

rubric.why: Schwann's conclusion concerned the cellular composition of animals.
rubric.description: States that Schwann concluded animals are made of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking Schwann with animals being composed of cells.

modelAnswer: Schleiden discovered that plants are made of cells.
Schwann discovered that animals are made of cells; together they proposed the cell theory.

items.followUp: How does cytokinesis take place in an animal cell?

rubric.why: In plant cells, cytokinesis begins with formation of a cell plate at the centre.
rubric.description: States that a cell plate forms at the equator or middle of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the cell plate and its central position.

rubric.why: The growing cell plate divides the cytoplasm and becomes the separating wall.
rubric.description: States that the cell plate grows outward and forms a new wall between the daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the plate's growth or its separation of the daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Vesicles gather at the equator of the plant cell and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outward and joins the cell membrane, forming a new cell wall between the daughter cells.

items.followUp: What is the effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme action?

rubric.why: Enzymes work most effectively within a particular pH range, with a specific optimum pH.
rubric.description: States that each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works best.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the optimum pH.

rubric.why: Moving away from the optimum changes the enzyme's activity; extreme pH can alter its shape.
rubric.description: States that activity decreases away from the optimum and/or extreme pH denatures the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing reduced activity or denaturation at unsuitable pH.

modelAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which its activity is greatest.
Above or below this pH, enzyme activity decreases; extreme pH can denature the enzyme.

items.followUp: Explain the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme specificity through the fit between substrate and active site.
rubric.description: States that the substrate fits the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the substrate's fit with the active site.

rubric.why: In the induced fit model, substrate binding causes a change in the enzyme's shape.
rubric.description: States that substrate binding changes the active site's shape to fit the substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the induced shape change.

modelAnswer: The enzyme's active site is not rigid; when the substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it.
An enzyme-substrate complex forms, after which the reaction occurs and products are released.

items.followUp: State the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Cellular respiration involves the breakdown or oxidation of food molecules.
rubric.description: Defines respiration as the breakdown or oxidation of glucose or food in cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the breakdown or oxidation of food.

rubric.why: The purpose of respiration is to make energy available to the cell.
rubric.description: States that respiration releases energy for cellular activities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the release of energy.

modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the series of reactions in cells in which glucose is broken down.
This process releases energy for the cell.

items.followUp: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The definition must identify photosynthesis as the process by which plants make glucose using light energy.
rubric.description: States that plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the process and its raw materials and energy source.

rubric.why: The balanced chemical equation gives the required reactants and products in the correct proportions.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation, with light and chlorophyll indicated over the arrow or in the answer.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

items.followUp: What is lactic acid fermentation, and in which cells does it occur?

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation is an anaerobic process commonly carried out by yeast.
rubric.description: States that yeast ferments glucose without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast and the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: The main products distinguish alcoholic fermentation from other forms of respiration.
rubric.description: Identifies ethanol and carbon dioxide as products of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products or giving the products in the equation.

modelAnswer: In the absence of oxygen, yeast breaks down glucose by alcoholic fermentation.
